steps.text: English has no sound like the Greek γ, and its name, gamma, tempts you to say it as the g of “go”. It is never that hard g. Before α, ο, ω, ου or a consonant it is a soft throaty g: the back of the tongue comes close to the roof of the mouth but never touches it, and the voice hums through the gap. Before an e or i sound (ε, αι, η, ι, υ, ει, οι) it is the y of “yes”, with a little hiss.

text.american: Start from the throaty ch of “chutzpah”, or of German “Bach”: the back of the tongue nearly touches the roof of the mouth and the air rubs through. Hold it, then hum while you hold it: the hum turns it into γ. Then say “yes” and lean on the y a little: that is γ before e and i, as in γῆ.
text.british: Start from the ch of Scottish “loch”, said as a Scot says it and not as “lock”: the back of the tongue nearly touches the roof of the mouth and the air rubs through. Hold it, then hum while you hold it: the hum turns it into γ. Then say “yes” and lean on the y a little: that is γ before e and i, as in γῆ.

steps.text: Listen to the soft throaty γ before α and ο in ἀγάπη and λόγος, and before ρ in γράφω; then to the y of γῆ, λέγει and γινώσκομεν, where an e or i sound follows. Neither is ever the g of “go”.

In the first two pairs γ stands against χ: the same place in the mouth, and only the voice humming through γ tells them apart. In the last two γ stands against nothing at all, so listen for it: an English ear lets the soft γ slip by.
Say each word after the voice. Keep the back of the tongue off the roof of the mouth: if you hear the g of “go”, it touched. Before e and i, a firm y.
This verse has both kinds, each γ marked: the soft throaty γ of ἀγάπη and ἀγαπῶμεν, and the y of γεγέννηται and γινώσκει. Hear it, then say it, with no hard g anywhere.
